title: Sunita the flower-scavenger
hook: a man of the lowest caste, sweeping discarded flowers, is invited to ordain (Theragatha, Sunita)

segments.voice: Yesterday: rajoharana, a clean cloth slowly soiled in a slow monk's hands. Your line: the cloth grows gray. Today, a man who carried away dead flowers.

Born in a low family. Poor. Little to eat. That's how Sunita describes himself in his verses in the Theragatha, the poems of the elder monks. His work was lowly too, he says: he carried away withered flowers, the ones people had thrown out. People despised him and looked down on him, and he kept his mind humble and bowed to many. Then one day he saw the Buddha walking into the chief city of Magadha, with the company of monks around him. Today, what happened on that street.
screen: `POOR, AND LITTLE TO EAT.` → `CARRYING AWAY DEAD FLOWERS.` → `THE BUDDHA ON THE STREET.`

segments.voice: First, the pole. Sunita sets down his carrying pole and goes to pay his respects. And in his verse, the Buddha, the highest of men, stops and stands still, out of compassion for him. Second, the question. Sunita bows at the Teacher's feet, stands to one side, and asks to go forth, to become a monk. Third, the answer. The Buddha, compassionate toward the whole world, says, come, monk. And Sunita says: that was my ordination. Two words, spoken on a street, to a man whose job was clearing away other people's dead flowers. Fourth, the end of the poem. He goes off alone into the forest and practices as the Teacher taught him, and the verses say he reached the end of the path. Then the gods come and honor him with joined palms, and the Buddha smiles and speaks a verse: by austerity, by the holy life, by restraint and taming, this is how one becomes a brahmin; this is the highest brahminhood. The word brahmin is still there, but in the Buddha's mouth it's about how someone lives, not the family they were born to. The man people stepped around becomes the one the gods bow to. And the first thing that happened to him wasn't a test. It was a welcome. The sweeper was welcome.
screen: `HE PUTS DOWN HIS POLE.` · `MAY I GO FORTH?` · `COME, MONK.` · `HONORED BY HOW HE LIVES.` · then, large: `THE SWEEPER WAS WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Picture the people your days pass by without a word: whoever empties the bins at work, cleans the restroom, drops off the delivery. Choose one face, or one role, and hold them in mind for a few breaths, the way the Buddha stopped on the street. Let a plain wish for their well-being come.
Sunita. The poor flower-scavenger, despised for his low birth, whom the Buddha stopped for and welcomed with two words: come, monk.
Your line: the sweeper was welcome. Honor, in that verse, comes from how a person lives. That's day seven hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Teachers retell Sunita's story when speaking of the Buddha's welcome to people of every background, and Sunita's verses are read as part of the Theragatha, the collection of poems by the early elder monks.

chat.says: Did the Buddha turn people away because of the family they were born into?
options: Not Sunita: poor and despised, he asked, and the Buddha said, come, monk.
Yes, low-born people could follow him only as lay supporters.
Only after they'd proved themselves first by years of tests.
chat.meaning: In his verses, Sunita, a despised flower-scavenger, asks to go forth, and the Buddha welcomes him: come, monk. That was his ordination.

notes: Theragatha (Sunita) paraphrased; Rhys Davids's 1913 Psalms of the Brethren could supply a quotable wording if a Keeper confirms it. Confirm verse numbers.

Confirm in the verses: low family, poor, little food; lowly work as a remover of withered flowers (pupphachaddaka); despised, humble, bowing to many; seeing the Buddha entering the chief city of Magadha with the sangha; setting down the carrying pole; the Buddha standing still out of compassion; 'come, bhikkhu' as his ordination; practice alone in the forest; Inda and Brahma honoring him; the Buddha's smile and the verse on austerity, holy life, restraint and taming as the highest brahminhood.
The index hook says 'the lowest caste'; the script follows the verses ('a low family') and does not name a caste.
The brahmin verse is presented as the text's redefinition of honor by conduct; it is not framed against any other tradition. Keeper to confirm the framing is fair.
